instructions: Slice the yellow onion thinly. Cut the carrots into thin half-moons. Cut the pork into thin bite-size slices, about 1/4 inch thick. Slice the green onions.

Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high. Add the pork and sprinkle over the 1/4 tsp salt. Cook for 3 minutes, stirring now and then, until the pork has lost its pink and is browning at the edges.
Add the onion and carrots. Cook for 4 minutes, until the onion is soft and a little golden.

Add 5 cups of water, the 5 tsp dashi powder, 2 tbsp soy sauce and 2 tbsp mirin. Bring it to a boil, skim off any foam, then turn the heat to medium-low and simmer for 8 minutes, until the carrots are tender.
Meanwhile, bring a second pot of water to a boil for the udon.
Turn the heat off under the soup. Ladle about 1 cup of the hot broth into a bowl, break the curry roux into it and whisk until it's smooth. Stir it back into the pot.
Put the soup back on low and simmer for 3 minutes, stirring, until it's lightly thickened and coats the back of a spoon.
Drop the udon into the boiling water and cook for 1 to 2 minutes, loosening the noodles with chopsticks, until they're separate and hot all the way through. Drain well and divide between 4 bowls.
Taste the soup. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Ladle the curry over the noodles and scatter over the green onions.

To pack it for lunch: let the soup cool, then pack it in a jar or thermos container and the drained noodles in a separate container. The soup keeps for 3 days in the fridge, and the noodles for 2. Reheat the soup until it's steaming, then pour it over the noodles.
method_notes: No version had 20 or more ratings, so this is a fallback and the weak lead is flagged: Norecipes (4.91 from 11 ratings) leads; the trusted cook RecipeTin Eats had no curry udon page. All versions agree on dashi, soy and mirin with curry, onion, and a thickening step; they differ on roux (Takes Two Eggs, Japanese Taste) versus curry powder with grated vegetables (Norecipes). I used the roux for a lunch-sized effort, thin pork as in Japanese Taste, and instant dashi powder, and left out the aburaage and sour cream.
